title: Scallion Crisp Mongolian Flank Tray
seoTitle: Scallion Crisp Mongolian Flank Tray | Firehall BBQ
shortDescription: Mongolian beef on the flat-top—crisp flank, glossy sauce, rice for ten
subtitle: Crisp flank strips, sweet-savory sauce, and scallions for ten
description: Flank steak sliced thin, dredged in cornstarch, and seared crisp on a ripping-hot flat-top, then tossed with a soy–brown sugar glaze, charred scallions, and a splash of black vinegar. The takeout classic, sized for a full crew.
equipment: Heavy pot with tight lid (for rice)

steps.title: Slice the flank thin and set the dredge
steps.instruction: Chill the flank steak in the freezer 20 minutes so it firms up, then slice ¼ inch thick against the grain — find the long muscle lines and cut across them, or every strip eats chewy. Toss the slices with the Shaoxing wine and 2 tablespoons of the soy sauce, rest 10 minutes, then toss with cornstarch until every piece wears a thin, tacky coat. That crust is what crisps on the hot metal and later grabs the sauce.

steps.title: Start the jasmine rice early
steps.instruction: Rinse the jasmine rice until the water runs nearly clear — surface starch is what turns a pot gummy. Add 5 cups water and a pinch of salt, bring to a boil, then cover and drop to low for 12 minutes. Kill the heat and let it steam 10 more without lifting the lid; peeking dumps the steam that finishes the top layer.

steps.title: Stir the sauce and stage the aromatics
steps.instruction: Whisk the remaining soy sauce, dark brown sugar, and 1 cup water until the sugar fully dissolves. Mince the ginger and garlic, tear the dried Thai chilies in half, and cut the scallions into 2-inch batons. Line everything up in bowls next to the flat-top — once the sauce hits hot metal it reduces in about 2 minutes, and there is no time to hunt for a cutting board.

steps.title: Get the griddle ripping hot
steps.instruction: Preheat the griddle on high 8–10 minutes to about 450°F — a drop of water should skitter and vanish within 2 seconds. Wipe on a thin film of peanut oil just before the first batch goes down; oil added too early smokes out and turns gummy. A surface that is not fully hot is the number-one reason the cornstarch crust comes out pale and soggy instead of crisp.

steps.title: Sear the beef in single layers
steps.instruction: Lay the flank strips flat in a single layer and leave them alone 2 minutes so a deep brown crust forms before you flip; move them early and the coating tears off. Flip and cook 1–2 minutes more until the edges crisp and the thickest strips read 145°F on an instant-read thermometer. Work in three or four batches — a crowded surface steams the meat gray. Pull each finished batch to a sheet pan.

steps.title: Bloom the aromatics and reduce the sauce
steps.instruction: Drop to medium, add the ginger, garlic, and torn Thai chilies to the oiled surface, and stir 30–45 seconds until fragrant but not browned — scorched garlic turns the whole batch bitter. Pour on the soy–sugar mixture and let it bubble 2–3 minutes until it reduces to a syrup thick enough that a spatula drag leaves a visible trail.

steps.title: Toss strips, scallions, and vinegar at the finish
steps.instruction: Return the seared strips and any juices, add the scallion batons, and toss 60–90 seconds until every piece is glossy and the scallions turn bright green but still have snap. Kill the heat and hit the pile with the Chinese black vinegar — a long sweet glaze needs that acid snap or the tray eats flat by the third bite.

steps.title: Build the trays over rice
steps.instruction: Fluff the rice with a fork and spread it into hotel pans, then pile the glazed strips and scallions over top so the sauce seeps down into the grains. Portion about 8 oz of meat per firefighter, and scatter any extra crisp scallion ends over the trays before you call the crew.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-cook: turn off direct heat and cover the Mongolian beef — hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven, never below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Log hold time on the pan with a grease pencil. If tones drop after service, cover hot food and keep sides on low heat or ice as appropriate. On return, spot-check proteins at safe internal temp before reopening the line.

steps.title: Pack down leftovers safely
steps.instruction: Cool Mongolian beef and hot components in shallow hotel pans within two hours — deep pots stay in the danger zone too long. Label with date; reheat proteins to 165°F minimum before second shift. Store cold components separately so textures survive overnight.

proTips: Freeze the flank 20 minutes before slicing — a firm steak cuts into even ¼-inch strips instead of ragged shreds.
Dredge in cornstarch right before the sear; coated strips that sit around turn gummy and never crisp.
If the glaze over-reduces into candy, whisk in a splash of hot water to bring it back to a pourable syrup.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run — never serve picked-over pans to late crew.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Log hold times on the pan with a grease pencil when tones drop mid-service.
Spot-check proteins with an instant-read thermometer before reopening the line after a call.
tonightSpread: Main: Crispy Mongolian beef with charred scallions
Sides: steamed jasmine rice, quick cucumber salad with rice vinegar
Condiments: extra dried chilies, toasted sesame seeds if the pantry has them
Set hot components closest to the crew; cold crunch and toppings at the far end of the line.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run.
leftovers: Cool Mongolian beef in shallow pans within two hours; label with date and reheat to 165°F before second shift.
Store cold sides separately — hot and cold stacked overnight ruins texture.
Re-crisp leftover strips in a hot dry skillet 2–3 minutes instead of the microwave — steam kills the crust.
Chop day-two leftovers into fried rice with extra scallions and a knob of ginger.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Takeout-counter crunch without the wok — the cornstarch crust stays crisp under a glossy sweet-savory glaze, and the sauce toss happens at service so nothing goes soggy while the crew lines up.
substitutions: Sirloin or skirt steak swaps 1:1 for flank — skirt cooks even faster, so pull it at the first sign of crisp edges.
No Shaoxing wine? Dry sherry matches closest; a splash of chicken broth works in a pinch with slightly less depth.
Coconut aminos swap 1:1 for soy sauce (gluten-free) — they run sweeter, so cut the brown sugar by a third.
No Chinese black vinegar? Rice vinegar plus a pinch of sugar lands in the same neighborhood.
mealPrepNotes: Slice flank thin against the grain and dredge just before searing. Sear in single layers at 450°F — never crowd the surface. Sauce toss happens at service; hold seared strips dry and covered up to 25 minutes.
